articles.title: ‘I came for a degree, ended up wanting to stay’: Zimbabwean student’s adorable love letter to India wins hearts
articles.summary: What if moving to another country for a degree leaves you wanting to stay forever?
articles.body: What if moving to another country for a degree leaves you wanting to stay forever?That seems to be what happened with Zimbabwean student Kalumba Mwale, whose post about his time in India has caught attention online. He described coming to India to study as a “mistake”, but anyone reading the rest of his post quickly realises that he wasn't complaining.Quite the opposite.For Mwale, what started as a decision to pursue an education turned into three years of food, travel, friendships and experiences that changed the way he looked at India.So, why did he call it a ‘mistake’?Mwale shared his experience on Instagram, explaining that India became much more than the place where he happened to study.“I came here for a degree… and ended up wanting to stay. India became much more than just the country where I studied,” he wrote.And then came his list of reasons.One of the first things he mentioned was food.Mwale said he had got used to how affordable eating out can be in India, to the point that he now looks at food prices back home differently.He also singled out UPI as something he didn't realise he'd miss so much.“UPI completely spoiled me. I can pay for chai, food, transport and almost anything with my phone,” he wrote.For someone used to paying for everyday things this way, going back to a different payment system can apparently feel like a step backwards.Biryani, butter chicken, dosa and momosThen there was the food.Mwale said he had become “addicted” to Indian food, naming biryani, butter chicken, dosa and momos among his favourites.And it wasn't just about eating.Travelling around India became another big part of his experience. Despite spending three years in the country, Mwale said he felt he had barely seen enough of it.“Even after three years, I feel like I’ve barely scratched the surface of India,” he wrote.From one region to another, he found himself experiencing different food, languages, traditions and ways of life.India became more than a study destinationPerhaps the biggest change, however, came from the people he met.Mwale said studying in India introduced him to people from different parts of the country as well as students from countries he never expected to meet.“Studying in India exposed me to different Indian cultures, languages and people from countries I never expected to meet,” he wrote.That experience appears to have changed his idea of what home means too.“I came here as a Zimbabwean student. Somewhere along the way, India became a place I genuinely feel connected to,” Mwale said.So the “mistake” wasn't really a mistake.He later clarified that he was being sarcastic. In fact, he described these experiences as some of the best things that happened because he chose to study in India.He came for a degree.But according to him, he ended up with much more: friendships, memories, travel experiences and a connection to a country he hadn't expected to call home.‘India is like a second home’The post drew plenty of warm reactions online, with Indian users welcoming Mwale and relating to his experience.“It’s always heartwarming to hear someone born abroad say they love the country I was born in,” one person commented.Another told him, “I think India is like a second home for you now!” and even suggested that he learn to cook Indian food or make reels around it.“Whoever comes to India once becomes a part of India forever,” another comment read.A user added, “Welcome, brother. If you welcome the change, you can treat India like a second home.”For Mwale, perhaps that's the real story behind the word “mistake”. He arrived in India expecting an education. Three years later, he found himself wondering if he wanted to leave at all.Get the latest movie news, reviews, and celebrity updates. Download the TOI App.

articles.title: How two brothers put the humble handpan on Bengluru’s musical map
articles.summary: Twenty-six handpans turned a Bengaluru festival stage into a sea of metallic sound.
articles.body: Twenty-six handpans turned a Bengaluru festival stage into a sea of metallic sound. At the centre of the 24-member ensemble were brothers, Ranganathan S, 15, and Sriniketan S, 11. They had spent months rehearsing, travelling across the city several times a week and helping coordinate compositions for the ensemble.At its debut public performance at Bengaluru's Ganesha Utsava, the ensemble played five songs with 26 handpans alongside mridangam, ghatam, drums, guitar, synth and djembe. Their repertoire included Carnatic compositions along with 'Varaha Roopam' from the film 'Kantara.'Led by the Nadamaya Brothers, who were playing two handpans each, the performance offered the city's growing handpan community an opportunity to demonstrate that an instrument still on the fringes of mainstream music can function as a lead instrument. Their journey began during the pandemic.Ranganathan, who was nine then, had already been experimenting with the keyboard when a neighbour invited him to see an unusual percussion instrument he had begun crafting.His first impression remains vivid. "It looked like a spaceship," he recalls. Intrigued by its shape and sound, he quickly picked up the basics. Within a few hours, he was exploring melodies on an instrument he had never encountered before. Soon, his younger brother followed.Sriniketan says he was initially drawn to the instrument because his elder brother was playing it. "I was inspired by watching my brother play the handpan. I have been learning to play the handpan for the past three years now. What I love most is that it combines percussion and melody, so you can play both at once without needing two separate instruments," he says.Today, both brothers practise for at least two hours every day, often spending considerably longer when preparing for a public performance. Ranganathan, having completed his Class 10 examinations ahead of schedule, has taken a gap year to focus entirely on music, combining handpan practice with Carnatic vocal training and Vedic studies.Age, however, is not the only reason why the brothers have attracted attention within the handpan community. Fellow performers describe them as among the country's most accomplished young handpan players. While other ensemble members handle rhythmic and harmonic layers, the brothers perform the lead melodies, navigating complex arrangements and Carnatic-inspired compositions on chromatic handpans carrying more than 40 notes.Their rise mirrors the growth of Bengaluru's handpan community itself.At the centre of this growth is Chirag Vaitheeswaran, founder of Chirp Handpans, regarded by the handpan community as one of India's pioneering indigenous handpan makers. His fascination with the instrument began in 2013, when he encountered one on a beach in Gokarna. At the time, handpans were difficult to obtain, with long international waiting lists and high import costs.He embarked on a painstaking quest to build one himself while working at Microsoft. For nearly two years, he estimates that he produced nearly 200 failed shells before crafting a successful instrument. His Bengaluru workshop now employs 14 artisans and has delivered more than 1,300 instruments crafted entirely from Indian-sourced materials.Making the instrument accessible contributed to the growth of Bengaluru's handpan community through workshops and impromptu jam sessions. Players began looking beyond the instrument's familiar association with meditation, yoga retreats, and ambient soundscapes."I truly believe this instrument has the power to touch people across age groups and backgrounds, and I'm excited to be part of a community that's helping introduce it to more people," says ensemble member, Shruthi Shetty.The ensemble itself is designed to highlight the melodic and rhythmic capabilities of the handpan, with different performers assigned roles like those in an orchestra. The arrangement, inspired partly by steel-pan ensembles in Trinidad and Tobago, seeks to demonstrate that the instrument can support complex musical performances rather than simply create atmosphere. That vision resonates strongly with Ranganathan.His ambition is to take Indian handpan music to international audiences and expand its repertoire through Carnatic music, film songs and original compositions. He believes familiarity is key: audiences first recognise a song and then begin paying attention to the instrument producing it. "If it stays in the background, it won't become famous," says the teenager. "I want it to become like the flute or the mandolin."What is a handpan?The handpan is still an unfamiliar instrument for many people. Resembling a metallic flying saucer, it is played entirely with the hands and produces deep, resonant tones that blend melody and rhythm. The handpan is tuned to a specific scale, allowing even first-time players to create harmonious sounds, making it accessible.Origin: Inspired by the steelpan from Trinidad and Tobago, as well as traditional instruments like the Indian ghatam and Indonesian gamelan, people across the world started refining and creating their own versions of handpans. The creators combined elements of the Caribbean steelpan (steel drum) with the Indian ghatam (a clay pot percussion instrument, mostly used in Carnatic music).Meaning of its name: "Hang" means "hand" in the Bernese German dialect, describing how the instrument is played.Material: It is built from two glued-together steel shells made of a treated metal, called nitrided steel.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Bengaluru | Silver Rate in Bengaluru | Bank Holidays in Bengaluru | Public Holidays in Bengaluru | Bengaluru AQI | Weather in Bengaluru | Petrol Price in Bengaluru | Diesel Price in Bengaluru | CNG Price in Bengaluru | LPG Price in BengaluruStay updated with the latest Bengaluru news. articles.summary: BENGALURU: A woman's frantic three-hour journey to cover just 19km through peak-hour Bengaluru traffic has drawn attention online after she shared a video
articles.body: BENGALURU: A woman's frantic three-hour journey to cover just 19km through peak-hour Bengaluru traffic has drawn attention online after she shared a video recounting how she raced against time to catch a train to Kerala.The woman said she started from Electronic City around 5pm to catch a 7pm train from Krishnarajapuram station, despite knowing that the train was already running two hours late.Heavy rain in Bengaluru further worsened the traffic, stretching what should have been a short journey into a three-hour ordeal.She said the 19km journey took more than three hours, leaving her and her fellow travellers convinced midway that they would miss the train.Bengaluru traffic puts train journey at riskAccording to her account, the worsening traffic led them to consider turning back. Not today.’" ‘Huge respect’ for Bengaluru commutersThe experience also left her expressing admiration for people who make long daily commutes through Bengaluru's traffic.She said she was not someone who could handle such a journey every day and had, over the last 10 years, tried to live within five kilometres of her workplace."Hopefully I can do it," she said, referring to continuing to stay close to work.She also hoped for better transport and road infrastructure in Bengaluru, while ending on a softer note about the city."whatever I complain about Bangalore I still love you Bangalore," she said.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Bengaluru | Silver Rate in Bengaluru | Bank Holidays in Bengaluru | Public Holidays in Bengaluru | Bengaluru AQI | Weather in Bengaluru | Petrol Price in Bengaluru | Diesel Price in Bengaluru | CNG Price in Bengaluru | LPG Price in BengaluruStay updated with the latest Bengaluru news. articles.title: Inside the ‘kill box’: The Yemenis who stayed behind in Houthi-held Mocha
articles.summary: Yemenis trapped in the Red Sea port city speak of deteriorating conditions there.
articles.body:
Nabil watched from his balcony as a column of displaced people passed by at dawn on September 10, hours before Houthi forces entered Mocha, a Yemeni city on the Red Sea.

“People were terrified. There was fear everywhere,” he said.

Nabil, a daily wage labourer in his 40s, did not join them. He still lives in Yakhtul, a village north of Mocha, alongside relatives, none of whom has left their homes.

“Displacement is humiliation and homelessness,” he said. “I haven’t done anything wrong, so I have nothing to be afraid of, and I don’t belong to any side.”

Weeks after the Houthis took Mocha from forces loyal to Yemen’s internationally recognised government, thousands of civilians remain in the district. The Houthis – an armed group that has controlled much of northern Yemen, including the capital, Sanaa, since September 2014 – have fought the government for more than a decade in a civil war that has drawn in a Saudi-led military coalition. No one knows how many people remain in Mocha, but according to Yemen’s last census in 2004 the city had 62,500 residents.

The government has declared Mocha a military zone and alleged that the Houthis have forced residents to demonstrate in support of the group or join its ranks.

Residents interviewed by Al Jazeera did not describe forced demonstrations, but one who asked not to be identified because he feared for his safety said three of his neighbours have been recruited and armed by the Houthis. They are now on the front lines fighting against government forces.

“Today my wife heard from a woman who came to our house that a Houthi-armed pick-up truck had kept coming to their home, wanting to recruit her sons, but she refused,” he said. “I know these people. They are our neighbours. One of her sons even spoke to me about it himself.”

The truck left after she refused, he said.

Mocha’s port lies about 75km (45 miles) north of the Bab al-Mandeb strait, a chokepoint for Red Sea shipping that the Houthis have repeatedly targeted since late 2023.

After government-aligned forces recaptured Mocha in 2017, the city became a refuge for Yemenis fleeing Houthi-controlled territory.

That changed in early September when fighting moved down the coast and families fled towards Aden, Taiz and Lahij. Many had already escaped Houthi rule once before.

On the evening of September 10, the government declared Mocha and its surroundings a “kill box”, a strike zone, warning that any Houthi movement there would be met with available firepower. Attacks began the following day.

Now residents say that leaving Mocha is almost impossible. “After the kill box was declared, the government opened the old al-Barh road so people could leave,” said Fuad, a 27-year-old pharmacist.

“Some got out, some were prevented by the Houthis and some stayed home, fearing the hardship of displacement.”

The Houthis have imposed a nighttime curfew on the city. Prices have soared, and power cuts have grown frequent, Nabil said.

A cooking gas cylinder has more than doubled in price to about 20,000 rials ($13), and a 50kg (110lb) sack of flour has risen by 8,000 rials ($5).

“A day’s work barely covers petrol and lunch,” he said. “Children have stopped going to school.”

Classrooms remain largely empty. “Parents and students are afraid of shelling or of their sons being thrown onto the front lines,” said Mansour, a teacher at a government secondary school who could not afford to flee with his family of seven.

“I am a teacher. I have nothing to do with politics,” he said. “In the end, we only die once.”

For Umm Khaled, a woman in her 60s whose husband is disabled and bedridden, leaving Mocha was never an option. “Where would I flee to? Look at my situation,” she said.

Her son, who had supported the family by fishing, joined the government-aligned National Resistance Forces for a monthly salary of 1,000 Saudi riyals ($267). He fled with them as the Houthis advanced, leaving behind his wife and two children, aged 15 and nine, in her care.

“Now they have fled, and we are lost,” she said. The local grocer has stopped extending credit, and the family survives on a sack of flour distributed by an aid group before the takeover. “Someone brings a fish, someone brings a yogurt and the rest is up to God,” she added.

Hassan, a 40-year-old fisherman who supports nine people, said he could not afford to leave the city. A ride to nearby Taiz costs up to 200,000 rials ($128). “Where would I go when I don’t even have my daily bread?” he asked.

Civilians have also been killed in the “kill zone”.

Before dawn on September 22, the bombing of a house in Mocha killed six members of one family , according to Mahmoud al-Otmi, a journalist with Saudi-owned Al-Hadath news channel whose relatives died.

Houthi-run media blamed Saudi air strikes. Saudi Arabia has not commented publicly.

Colonel Abdulbaset al-Bahr, deputy head of moral guidance in the government’s Taiz military command, said the kill box targets Houthi fighters.

“The kill box is for killing the militia, not civilians,” he said. “The statement did not ask civilians to leave the kill box area. Rather it asked them to stay in their homes and keep away from the militia’s barracks, positions and military gatherings.”

Sultan Mahmoud, the government-appointed director of the Mocha district, said no route out of the city was entirely safe as he accused the Houthis of targeting civilians.

Healthcare has nearly collapsed. On the day Houthi forces entered the city, Doctors Without Borders , also known by its French acronym MSF, said nearly all health facilities except Mocha General Hospital had stopped functioning. This was largely because staff had fled although about 30 health workers stayed behind, MSF told The National newspaper.

Residents said conditions in Mocha have since worsened.

“Doctors who were paid by organisations have stopped working because there are no salaries,” Nabil said. Fuad said the Houthis had placed hospitals under a security cordon and some medical equipment had been moved to Sanaa.

Aid has barely reached those who have stayed. Najib al-Saadi, head of the government’s executive unit for displacement camps, said his unit could not reach those in need.

“It is certain that there are families who could not flee because of poverty,” he said, accusing the Houthis of blocking humanitarian work. The International Committee of the Red Cross declined to comment.

In Yakhtul, Nabil said he would not leave, even if the fighting intensifies. “First, money is an obstacle,” he said. “And the house would be looted.”

articles.title: U.S. Marine arrested on suspicion of killing Japanese woman in Okinawa
articles.summary: A United States service member is in custody on suspicion of killing a Japanese national on the island of Okinawa.
articles.body: A United States service member is in custody on suspicion of killing a Japanese national on the island of Okinawa. Lance Cpl. Devin Jacob Ballard, 20, is suspected of killing Anna Yagi, 39, in a hotel in Naha, the capital of the southernmost prefecture, on Saturday and taking her wallet and backpack, ​local police told the Reuters news agency. Ballard denied the allegations, police said. The Marine was stationed at Futenma Air Station on Okinawa Island, police said, adding that he was arrested at 1 a.m. local time Sunday. “An investigation is underway to determine the facts of the case, the United States is communicating and cooperating with the Government of Japan and local authorities,” the U.S. Embassy in Tokyo said Sunday in a post on X. Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi described the death as an alleged robbery and murder. “The occurrence of such an extremely brutal and heinous incident is a matter of profound regret, and as the Government of Japan, we have lodged a strong protest with the U.S. side,” she said on social media. Japan’s Ministry of Defense said it was “deeply outraged by the extremely brutal and heinous crime committed by a U.S. Marine.” It said on X that it had made “a firm demand for stricter discipline, thorough measures to prevent recurrence.” The III Marine Expeditionary Force, a combat force of the U.S. Marine Corps headquartered in Okinawa, said it was cooperating with Japanese authorities in response to “allegations of serious criminal actions by a Marine.” “The Marine Corps takes these allegations very seriously and expects every Marine to adhere to the highest standards of behavior,” it posted on X. “The Marine is in custody of local authorities while investigations proceed.” Approached for further comment, the Pentagon referred NBC News to the Marines’ statement. U.S. Ambassador to Japan George Glass said he had spoken with Japan’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Okinawa Gov. Genta Koja, “pledging full cooperation as the investigation continues.” There are 18,000 U.S. Marines based in Japan, the majority of them stationed in Okinawa, just 60 miles from Taiwan at its closest point. The U.S. held the island from the end of World War II until 1972, and the presence of the U.S. military has often stirred resentment among residents. The 1995 abduction and rape of a 12-year-old girl by three U.S. servicemen sparked mass protests, as tens of thousands of people took to the streets, forcing Washington and Tokyo to discuss ways to reduce the U.S. military presence on the island.

images.caption: A general view of the U.S. Marine Corps Air Station Futenma from Kakazutakadai Park in Ginowan, Okinawa prefecture. For decades, residents of Japan's Okinawa have strongly opposed the U.S. military bases that dot the region.

articles.title: Russian drone slams into Kyiv bridge in escalating campaign as Germany’s chancellor arrives to airsirens and explosions
articles.summary: A Russian drone struck a major bridge in the Ukrainian capital of Kyiv on Sunday as German Chancellor Friedrich Merz arrived in the city to the sound of air raid sirens, explosions and air defense systems being activated.
articles.body: A Russian drone struck a major bridge in the Ukrainian capital of Kyiv on Sunday as German Chancellor Friedrich Merz arrived in the city to the sound of air raid sirens, explosions and air defense systems being activated. Merz is in Kyiv to display support for Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky amid Russia’s escalation of strikes on the city. “Ukraine needs all our support in the coming weeks,” Merz said. Highlighting attacks on Ukraine’s towns, residential buildings and energy, he said: “If Russia is not stopped, sooner or later its war machine will turn ⁠against us.” Video footage from Sunday morning’s strike showed the moment the city’s Northern Bridge was attacked, sparking a huge plume of fire and black smoke while cars were still traveling across. Two people were injured, the city’s mayor, Vitaliy Klitschko said. It is the second time the Northern Bridge has been hit in as many days. On Thursday and Friday, Kyiv’s Southern Bridge, which serves ground transportation and the city’s subway system, was hit five times in less than 24 hours. Ukrainian officials have said that Russian strikes on the capital’s infrastructure are attempting to cut the capital into two, as Kyiv is split along the Dnipro River, with businesses offices and government institutions on the right back, and the left bank mostly residential. Kyiv plans to start building several alternative crossings over the Dnipro in case the attacks on the bridges continue, the minister of infrastructure said Sunday. Russia’s defense ministry said it struck the Northern Bridge on Sunday, saying that it was targeting a route used for transporting troops and military equipment. It added that two cargo vessels carrying military equipment to the port of Odesa were struck. On Saturday the Russian Ministry of Defense said that it also targeted a logistics center in the Kyiv region. ‘Decisive weeks ahead’ Merz visited Kyiv alongside his Minister for Economic Affairs and Energy, Katarina Reiche, despite warnings from Russia on Saturday that foreign visitors and dignitaries to the Ukrainian capital are not safe amid an onslaught of Russian attacks. Zelensky and Merz are tying up a significant defense and industrial partnership, which will see the two countries finalize a deal for the production of drones and missiles. Berlin is also expected to release €1 billion ($1.13 billion) in military aid and €350 million ($390 million) for repairs to Ukraine’s damaged energy infrastructure, German government officials said. Zelensky has warned that Ukraine’s defensive need is expanding amid Russia’s accelerated air campaign, which has seen Moscow fire high-speed, jet-powered Shahed-type drones that can bypass some of Ukraine’s air defense systems and exploit its lack of interceptors. Earlier on Sunday, Merz said that Ukraine “is facing decisive weeks ahead.” Writing on X, he said: “I have traveled to Kyiv today with the message: You can rely on us.” Meanwhile, there appears to be no immediate respite for Kyiv’s three million residents, with Moscow on Sunday saying that it will only intensify its strikes targeting the capital and other cities. “Strikes by the Armed Forces of the Russian Federation against military and military-industrial facilities, as well as associated infrastructure in Kyiv and other regions of Ukraine, will be intensified,” the ministry said. Russia’s renewed threat follows an interview Zelensky gave to Reuters news on Saturday, where he outlined that he plans to double down on attacks on oil refineries. “We have to respond in any way (we can). With their attacks on our energy, we have to respond on their energy. First of all, oil refiners, etc. – what gives money to them for this war,” Zelensky said. His comments come despite the urging of US President Donald Trump, who recently asked Ukraine to stay away from attacks on Russia’s oil infrastructure, claiming it was sending global oil prices surging. CNN’s Kara Fox and Farida Elsebai contributed reporting.

articles.title: Trump’s nominee for Hostage Affairs envoy faces scrutiny on controversial Russia plan
articles.summary: President Trump is tapping his charismatic, straight-talking former lawyer, who has helped free hundreds of political prisoners from Belarus, to serve as the U.S. official charged with bringing home unjustly detained Americans abroad. John Coale, who serves as special envoy to Belarus, has detailed “vodka infused” negotiations with that country’s authoritarian leader, Alexander Lukashenko, to…
articles.body:
President Trump is tapping his charismatic, straight-talking former lawyer, who has helped free hundreds of political prisoners from Belarus, to serve as the U.S. official charged with bringing home unjustly detained Americans abroad.

John Coale, who serves as special envoy to Belarus, has detailed “vodka infused” negotiations with that country’s authoritarian leader, Alexander Lukashenko, to establish a back channel to Russian President Vladimir Putin and the release of high-profile political dissidents in the country. Coale’s diplomacy has included providing Lukashenko access to popular GLP-1 weight loss medication, as well as sanctions relief.

Trump nominated Coale for Special Envoy for Hostage Affairs (SPEHA) on Monday, a position carrying the rank of ambassador and requiring Senate-confirmation.

Coale is reportedly looking to replicate his Belarus strategy with Putin, proposing that the White House ease sanctions on Russia in exchange for releasing political prisoners.

It’s a controversial plan that will be at the forefront of an appearance before the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, which will consider his nomination.

“I think there are some tough questions that John Coale needs to answer,” Sen. Jeanne Shaheen (D-N.H.), the outgoing ranking member of the panel, told The Hill.

She commended Coale’s willingness to talk “to people on both sides of the aisle,” but called sanctions relief on Russia “unacceptable.”

It’s unclear, however if Shaheen, who is retiring after this Congress, will get the chance to question him about it.

The bureaucracy required ahead of a confirmation hearing, the panel’s workload and the scheduling of the lame duck Senate session after the midterm elections are all factors in whether Coale will come before the committee before the end of the year.

Sen. Bill Hagerty (R-Tenn.), a Foreign Relations member who said he was not familiar with Coale, rejected commenting on the strategy of easing sanctions on Russia, calling negotiations for people’s lives “extraordinarily sensitive.”

“I’m not going to comment in the media about this, or about undercutting him or supporting him, anything like that,” Hagerty said.

But Sen. Pete Ricketts (Neb.), the second-highest ranking Republican on the committee, rejected any sanctions relief on Moscow when asked for his reaction to the proposed strategy.

“I would advise keeping the sanctions on,” he said, calling Putin “a dictator.”

“We need to keep punching him in the nose.”

The White House says that Trump is committed to playing a constructive role in ending the war between Russia and Ukraine.

“The President wants this war settled so the senseless killing ends,” a White House official told The Hill.

Trump “remains optimistic that we’ll ultimately get a peace deal done.”

The Hill has also reached out to a representative for Coale for comment.

Coale, a former anti-tobacco litigator, earned Trump tens of millions of dollars in settlements from social media companies after the president was banned following the January 6, 2021 attack on the Capitol by his supporters.

Brought into Trump’s second term as a deputy envoy for Ukraine, Coale was instead dispatched to Minsk throughout 2025 to engage Lukashenko as a backchannel to Putin, amid early efforts to end Russia’s war against Ukraine.

The U.S. strategy marked a shift from what had been a campaign of isolation and maximum pressure through sanctions, imposed after Lukashenko carried out a violent crackdown on protesters and the political opposition following contested presidential elections in 2020.

Lukashenko’s release of political prisoners has earned Trump’s praise, with the president offering the chance for an in-person meeting and recently announcing a “massive Deal” to purchase potash fertilizer from the country as an alternative to Canada amid a trade war. Although Lukashenko publicly cast doubt on that agreement , regional experts view that as part of the Belarusian leader’s negotiating tactics.

Still, Trump delights in the high-profile acclaim of freeing Americans and others wrongly imprisoned around the world. The administration says the president has freed approximately 100 Americans unjustly detained, but Trump’s intervention has also secured the release of Israeli hostages held by Hamas in the Gaza Strip, a dual Israeli-Russian citizen held by an Iranian-backed militia in Iraq and a Chinese Christian pastor imprisoned in China, to name a few.

As SPEHA, Coale’s file would expand from Belarus to advocating the release of dozens of American hostages and wrongful detention cases globally, engaging authoritarian leaders and terrorist organizations around the world.

This includes Americans held by U.S. adversaries, such as Russia, China, the Taliban in Afghanistan and the Islamic Republic in Iran. Americans are also held by U.S. allies and partners: Turkey, Saudi Arabia, Egypt, the UAE, Syria and Cambodia, according to the Foley Foundation , a nonprofit organization that advocates for the release of Americans held abroad.

Coale’s ability to ingratiate himself with Lukashenko and get results signals a particular knack for sensitive diplomacy. Lukashenko is described as a cunning and ruthless authoritarian leader and tough negotiating partner.

Coale, in an interview with The New York Times published in August, said he was advised to “yuk it up” with Lukashenko and curried favor by egging a vulgar bashing of European leaders.

“I knew that’s what he wanted to hear, something like that, to lighten everything up,” Coale told the Times.

But a key part of Coale’s success is also tied to his close coordination with experts in the State Department, in particular Deputy Assistant Secretary in the Bureau of European and Eurasian Affairs Chris Smith, who spearheaded re-engagement with Lukashenko.

“John Coale managed to get more political prisoners released than any other, 500 people, that’s to his credit,” said Daniel Fried, a distinguished fellow with the Atlantic Council who has spoken with Coale and engaged with the Belarusian opposition in exile.

“The other thing to John Coale’s credit, and speaks well of him, he had not only the judgement, but the self-confidence, in a good way,” to work with experts and avoid Lukashenko’s traps, Fried continued.

Still, treating human lives as bargaining chips for sanctions relief is a controversial strategy.

There’s fraught debate among the Belarusian diaspora over the impact of the sanctions lifting regarding how much it empowers Lukashenko or benefits Russia in its war against Ukraine. And while activists celebrate the lives that were saved, Lukashenko is filling prisons at the same time he is emptying them out.

“Sanctions are leverage, and if limited, reversible steps can help bring people home, that leverage can be used strategically,” Svetlana Tsikhanouskaya, Belarus’s opposition leader in exile, said in a statement to The Hill earlier this month, responding to Coale facilitating the release of 25 more people from Lukashenko’s jails on Sept. 16.

“And we must distinguish between sanctions. Human rights sanctions can be discussed with a humanitarian track. Sanctions related to Russia’s war, military cooperation and threats to European security are different,” she said.

Replicating the Belarus strategy to Russia is even more controversial.

Ukraine opposes any sanctions relief on Russia and is advocating for the blacklisting of several more entities and individuals following Trump signing into law the Sanctioning Russia Act of 2026, said Denys Sienik, chargé d’affaires for Ukraine’s embassy in Washington.

“Russia’s strategy of missile and drone attacks and increasing number of civilian casualties show that the time for any sanctions relief in Russia hasn’t come,” Sienik said in a statement to The Hill.

A major feature of the Sanctioning Russia Act is providing Trump tariff authorities on the five countries purchasing the majority of Russia’s energy exports. But the bill also provides additional sanctions against individuals and entities supporting the Russian government and its shadow-fleet of oil and gas tankers. And it provides tariff authorities on countries helping Russia evade sanctions.

Trump faces a mid-October deadline to inform Congress whether he is imposing tariffs and sanctions or issuing a waiver, and why.

Fried, from the Atlantic Council, said the large bipartisan and bicameral coalition that supported the Graham sanctions bill would likely push back on the “dumb” idea of sanctions relief on Russia. Selective sanctions-lifting on Lukashenko is not the same as easing penalties on Putin that would have direct consequence on Russia’s ability to wage war in Ukraine, he argued.

“Coale did a credible job in Belarus,” Fried said. “Applying that to Russia does not work. I think that’s dumb.”

articles.title: Inside the ‘Americanization’ of French dining
articles.summary: The arrival of elements of North American dining culture in France is being met with a mix of curiosity, reluctance — and resistance.
articles.body: Over the past year, an all-American-style diner serving Italian-American dishes became one of the most viral dining destinations in Paris. Inside Red Sauce, red velvet banquettes, neon signs, rotating ceiling fans, Formica tables topped with vintage salt and pepper shakers and bottles of Tabasco sauce recreate the look and feel of a diner that would fit right in on “The Sopranos.” Racks of Detroit-style pepperoni pizza topped with jalapeños and hot honey, and plates groaning with giant meatballs and eggplant parmigiana are passed out by young servers with faint Italian accents to tables of chattering French diners. Red Sauce is one of dozens of American-inspired dining experiences that have popped up around the French capital in recent years. Alongside New York-style pizzas sold by the slice, smash burgers and donuts, Parisians have also been introduced to regional American cuisines like Texas barbecue, Southern-style fried chicken and waffles and seafood boils, complete with plastic gloves and paper bibs. But while American specialties have found legitimacy in France through the power of social media and savvy marketing, the cross-Atlantic arrival of other elements of North American dining culture is being met with a mix of curiosity, reluctance — and resistance. There’s the earlier dinner hour, which aligns with North American (and also Asian and Scandinavian) culture, a trend that has French newspaper Le Figaro wondering if it’s just “a passing fad or the start of a shift in habits?” There’s also the shortened, takeout lunch break replacing leisurely, multi-course restaurant lunches, as glamorized by the Netflix series “Emily in Paris.” Perhaps most controversial and, some say, the most insidious of all, is the growing adoption of digital tipping and tipping culture in general across France. It’s a shift that some deplore as the “Americanization” of French restaurant culture, which has become the subject of mainstream news and talk shows in recent years. “It’s a form of Americanization of French society,” said philosopher Jean-Loup Bonnamy, on a 2024 episode of the French talk show “Les Grandes Gueules” (“Big Mouths”) dedicated to the topic. “It’s the culture of ‘tipping’ and it’s a servile and misunderstood form of Americanization.” The rise of tipping prompts Unlike the US, tipping in France has never been considered an obligation, as servers are paid minimum wage. A 15% service charge, or service compris, is added to restaurant bills, which is used to pay staff salaries. If diners are feeling generous or had a particularly good experience, they may round up the bill and leave the change for their coffee, or a few euros at a cafe or bistro. As Elisabeth Debourse, editor-in-chief of the influential restaurant guide Le Fooding for France and Belgium, points out, the French word for a tip, pourboire, is a compound word and literally means “to drink.” “In France, tip is traditionally the change you have in your pocket and that you leave on the table for staff to buy themselves a drink later,” she says. But since the arrival of digital tipping options on card machines and QR codes over the last few years, tipping culture has shifted in France. Tipping prompts are now everywhere. Along with tip jars placed beside cash registers, customers are prompted to leave a 5% to 20% gratuity on their restaurant bills, but also on their fast-food takeout and coffees to-go when paying via card machines. In a recent column for Radio France, French journalist Frédéric Martel describes digital tipping as abusive, misleading and even “theft,” given that service is already included. He also called for a 5% cap on French tipping. “In the age of digital payments, it is high time to regulate abusive restaurant practices to reassure customers and remain faithful to the French spirit of service being included,” Martel writes. On social media and online forums, some French users call the emergence of digital tipping a scam that benefits restaurants and commission-earning payment platforms more than servers. Some resent the feeling of being pressured into tipping while servers hover over them with the payment machines. “When I get the tipping system on the digital app, I systematically refuse it because I’m afraid that it will lead back to the same system as in the US,” Rose Camara, a French woman in Lyon who dines out regularly, tells CNN. For Camara, it’s a matter of principle: servers should be paid a fair wage by their employer and the burden shouldn’t fall to customers, she said. The English teacher has no qualms about tipping for good service, but said she resents the digital tipping system because it feels forced, with tips dictated by a machine with predetermined percentages. Likewise, tipping can make settling up uncomfortable when dining out with friends. “It’s a heavy toll for some people,” she said. “I know some of my friends have to be really careful about how much they spend so asking them to give 10 or even 5% extra can be a lot for them and they don’t feel at ease.” ‘Tipping is supposed to be at the customer’s discretion’ Christophe Souques is a restaurateur with seven cafes and pubs across the south of France in cities like Toulouse, Cannes and Nice, where he’s best known for Ma Nolan’s Irish pubs. He says he started to notice generous North American-style tipping in his restaurants in the 1990s, when an uptick in direct international flights brought planeloads of wealthy American and Canadian tourists to the French Riviera. “Anglophone culture brought tipping to France. That’s very clear,” Souques tells CNN. As Souques explains, digital gratuities on card readers were widely adopted after the French government announced that card-based tipping — which until then was taxed as part of a restaurant’s revenue — would become tax-exempt as of 2022. According to a June report from payment platform provider Lightspeed, the percentage of digital transactions that involved an added customer gratuity rose from 4% in 2023, to nearly 10% in 2025. For the report, Lightspeed looked at tipping trends across 1,500 restaurants in France that use the company’s payment platforms from June 2023 to August 2025. But it’s a trend that some restaurateurs, like Souques, can’t get behind. Though both digital and cash tips are tax-free until the end of 2028, Souques, who is also the president of the Union of Hospitality Trades and Industries for the local Nice-area chapter, worries that digitized gratuities will make it easier for a government tax grab in the future. Furthermore, it’s just plain tacky, he says. He has eliminated the option at all his restaurants. “Tipping is supposed to be at the customer’s discretion. But forcing customers to choose from amounts displayed on a card machine violates their privacy and their right to decide,” he says. “It feels aggressive. and it’s shocking … It breaks the rapport between the server and customer.” That’s because restaurant service culture in France is less transactional than in North America, where servers work mostly for tips, and where the average service style — personal introductions, frequent check-ins, product upsells — can be viewed as over-the-top for Europeans. Souques describes French service culture as efficient, professional and discreet. So when a rapport is established between servers and customers, the connection is genuine, he says. Throw in “rude” request for a gratuity, and the connection is shattered. “It stops being about friendliness or a human connection. It becomes purely about money and becomes a financial transaction between the server and the customer,” Souques says. By the same token, French-style discretion can be interpreted by American visitors as inattentive and rude. After having traveled to Canada, Camara found North American-style service “overwhelming” compared to the more reserved service culture she was used to in France. But after a recent dining experience in Paris with a particularly playful and bubbly server, she realized that’s changing too. “Ten to 15 years ago, waiters here were really discreet and wouldn’t engage. Now, we see younger servers coming, introducing themselves and engaging in small talk.” ‘I don’t think it’s elegant’ Priscilla Quang has the added perspective of a chef and restaurateur who lived in New York, San Francisco and Hong Kong before moving back to Paris, where she runs two acclaimed restaurants. In 2024, she opened Trâm 130, a French- and Asian-influenced neo-bistro, and in July, Trâmette, a smaller, casual “deli counter” space inspired by the delis she used to frequent while living in the US. (Trâm is Quang’s first name in Vietnamese and is pronounced Tiam). But while the design of Trâmette was inspired by an American concept, Quang hasn’t been fully converted to American-style tipping: she has banned it outright at Trâm 130, and reluctantly installed the payment option at Trâmette. “I flatly refused to implement that at my first restaurant. I don’t think it’s elegant to have a ‘tip’ button right under your nose when paying the bill, especially since the average check at that first place is a bit higher,” Quang says. At Trâmette, Quang decided to test out the gratuity payment option — but only for guests with whom the staff may have struck a particularly good rapport. Otherwise, two out of three times, waitstaff will manually pass over the tipping prompt themselves before presenting the card reader to guests, she said. Quang estimates that about 20% of her customers tip and mostly for dinner service. “It’s not an automatic reflex at all for the French,” she says. “And when they do tip, they leave usually €2 to €5 ($2.30 to $5.80). We still don’t have that ingrained habit of tipping at all.” Le Fooding editor Debourse, who lives in Belgium but works half the week in Paris and eats out on average three times a week, agrees and points out that the proliferation of card readers hasn’t translated into widespread tipping. This is especially true in the current economy where purchasing power has diminished. Early dinner, quick lunch But it’s not just tipping culture that is making its way across the Atlantic. Dinner hour, which traditionally starts around 7:30 p.m. and peaks around 8 p.m. in France, is also seeing a small shift in the French capital. A new generation of restaurants including both Trâm addresses, Red Sauce and Bittikesu, another critically acclaimed newcomer this year, are opening as early as 6:30 p.m., aligning more with North American dinner times. For Canadian chef Jules St-Cyr, who opened his gastronomic counter restaurant Bittikesu in April, offering a 6:30 p.m. seating was about logistics, as the 15-course tasting menu lasts about 2.5 hours. The second seating is at 9 p.m. and each seating has a maximum of 10 guests. But the move was also about striking a work-life balance. “I don’t want our staff and our team to finish very late. It’s not worth it in the long term.” The first time slot might be a mix of tourists who are used to earlier dinner times and a few French guests, St-Cyr says. But there’s still quite a few French people who balk at the idea of eating that early and “don’t even want to hear it,” he adds. The fabled French, wine-fueled, two-hour lunch is also looking more like the North American lunch hour, with the demands of modern life shortening breaks, and fast food replacing restaurant meals. It’s also a big reason Quang decided against opening her gastronomic restaurant for lunch: the French are drinking less at lunch (alcohol is the most profitable part of a restaurant business), and overall budgets are shrinking. “The business lunch is disappearing,” Quang says. As to whether the current geopolitical climate and anti-American sentiment could affect the French appetite for all things American, Debourse, whose 2023 book “American appétit” explores American food culture, says that the French are able to keep politics and American pop culture — including American food culture — separate. “For the French, there’s no connection between enjoying things that stem from … American soft power and current American politics.”

articles.title: What are the five questions being asked regarding the Flydubai attack?
articles.summary: As investigations are conducted, official versions of the incident have come under scrutiny.
articles.body:
An attack by the copilot on the pilot during a Flydubai flight has raised many questions regarding aviation security, and some of the official versions of the incident have come under scrutiny from online commentators and aviation enthusiasts.

About two and a half hours after Flight FZ1073 departed from Dubai International Airport on Wednesday, it went into a sharp descent before eventually making an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia.

Media reports said the copilot attacked Captain Smit Machchhar. Passengers were able to overpower the copilot, identified by media as Hamam al-Hammami , after Machchhar managed to open the cockpit door during the attack, which the prosecutor general of the United Arab Emirates said was carried out with the cockpit’s crash axe.

While investigators continue working to establish a motive for the attack, several questions have arisen about the incident more generally across social media.

Here are five questions that are being asked:

Why was al-Hammami allowed to fly despite being flagged over security concerns?

Al-Hammami has been identified as an Omani national, according to media reports.

On Friday, The Wall Street Journal quoted unnamed sources as saying that Omani authorities previously blocked the suspect from flying in the country due to concerns over his ideological views.

On Saturday, CNN reported, quoting a regional diplomatic source, that the copilot had also been removed from flight training over similar concerns and was later reassigned to another position.

It added, quoting two sources familiar with the matter, that the pilot was removed from a job at Oman’s national airline last year over concerns about his views.

It remains unclear how al-Hammami managed to get the Flydubai route despite these security concerns.

The possibility of a plumber stabilising plane before reserve pilots stepped in

Reports have emerged that Machchhar managed to open the cockpit door while covered in blood, allowing passengers to subdue the copilot.

One of those who subdued al-Hammami was Yaniv Hayoun, whom Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu described as a plumber.

In a video with Netanyahu, who met him at the airport, Hayoun, 50, was asked how he knew what to do at the plane’s controls before another pilot took control. He said: “I watch Air Crash Investigation, Mr Prime Minister.”

“I jumped back, grabbed the controls and started pulling back the handles” the way he had seen in the Canadian investigation show, in which experts analyse plane crashes.

People on social media have questioned how a plumber could have handled an aircraft in the air.

No report of mass injuries despite fall of 5,180 metres

According to the flight-tracking website Flightradar24, the Flydubai flight rapidly descended about two and a half hours after takeoff, dropping more than 5,180 metres (17,000ft) in less than two minutes.

While the midair drop caused mass panic among passengers, no one was reportedly harmed, according to the publicly available information about the incident. An Air India flight that dropped 90 metres (300ft) during turbulence in August injured at least 17 passengers.

A flight instructor, who recreated the Flydubai jet’s near-vertical dive in a simulator, said the plane would have exceeded its maximum structural speed and anything unsecured would have flown all over the cabin during the recovery’s negative G-forces.

Why was the copilot allowed to fly despite being an Omani national?

Israel does not have official diplomatic relations with Oman, and Netanyahu has previously said such countries were not generally allowed to operate flights to Israel.

On Friday, Netanyahu said Israel was looking into whether the copilot had acted under anyone’s direction, warning that anyone involved would pay a “heavy price”.

On Saturday, the Israeli newspaper Haaretz reported that government officials had received in advance the list of crew members and passengers who were on the flight, including the Omani copilot.

Security sources told Haaretz that the government bodies responsible for monitoring and checking foreign flight crews landing in Israel are the Ministry of Transport and Road Safety’s Security Department and the security agency Mossad.

According to The Times of Israel, Machchhar spoke to Netanyahu on Saturday. He told the prime minister that al-Hammami had asked to pray before the attack. Four or five minutes later, Machchhar was hit with “a big blow” to the back of his head, he said.

The flight departed from the UAE at 7:05am (03:05 GMT). The attack reportedly took place about two and a half hours later (05:35 GMT).

The predawn prayer time in the Emirates on Wednesday was 04:51am (12:51 GMT), which would mean al-Hammami’s prayer did not align with Islamic prayer times.

However, al-Hammami could also have been performing a different personal prayer before the attack.

Bora, AAP leaders and activist Yogendra Yadav were among those detained that day.Police had denied permission for Friday's gathering and deployed additional personnel in central Delhi. articles.title: Dodik declared Bosnia ‘dead’. Irrelevant rhetoric or serious threat?
articles.summary: Bosnian Serb leader’s controversial comments ahead of Bosnia and Herzegovina’s high-stakes elections.
articles.body:
Speaking at the final rally of his right-wing alliance ahead of Bosnia’s October 4 election, Bosnian Serb leader Milorad Dodik delivered a predictably controversial statement.

“Bosnia-Herzegovina is dead. It is an impossible country, it makes no sense,” Dodik told supporters of the Alliance of Independent Social Democrats (SNSD) party in Banja Luka on Friday.

“It is now nothing more than an empty shell … for those who are trying to keep it alive, so they can prove themselves right about something,” said the former president of Republika Srpska, who is known for frequent separatist threats and for challenging the country’s constitution.

Dodik’s comments came as Bosnia remains deeply divided over its political future more than three decades since the 1995 Dayton peace agreement. It split the country into two semi-autonomous parts – the Serb-majority Republika Srpska entity and the Federation entity, where most Bosniaks and Croats live.

The agreement ended the 1992–95 Bosnian War and established a political framework for power-sharing among Muslim Bosniaks, Orthodox Serbs and Catholic Croats.

On Sunday, voters across the country cast ballots to elect the three members of Bosnia and Herzegovina’s multiethnic presidency, representatives to the national parliament and leaders of institutions in the country’s two entities.

Dodik himself is not on the ballot after being stripped of his post last year, following his conviction for refusing to carry out decisions issued by Christian Schmidt, the international peace envoy who oversees the implementation of the Dayton peace agreement.

Elvis Fejzic, a professor at the Faculty of Political Science in Sarajevo, said attempts by figures such as Dodik to dismantle Bosnia and Herzegovina amount to “populist rhetoric”.

“Politicians and political parties that act unconstitutionally do not determine the fate of Bosnia and Herzegovina,” Fejzic told Al Jazeera, arguing that Bosnia and Herzegovina’s status as a UN member and internationally recognised state is secure.

“Bosnia and Herzegovina … will outlive all those who, through inflammatory statements, seek to obstruct its path towards integration and development,” he said. “Their statements have no political relevance whatsoever.”

Political analyst Tanja Topic said that while Dodik was not officially a candidate, he remained a central figure in the campaign and sought to present himself as a “senior official in international relations”.

Topic told Al Jazeera that the election result could produce several political scenarios in Bosnia and Herzegovina, from “cohabitation in Republika Srpska”, through the formation of a grand coalition, to a “blockage at the state level and the Council of Ministers continuing to operate in a caretaker capacity”.

Dodik’s rhetoric marks ‘long escalation’

Expert Adnan Cerimagic said Dodik’s rhetoric should be taken “seriously” and viewed as part of a “long escalation” rather than a reflection of the country’s current reality.

“For the past four years, his moves against the Dayton order and against Bosnia’s EU and NATO path have reached a new and dangerous level: in March 2025 the country came close to an armed standoff between Republika Srpska and state police,” Cerimagic, a senior analyst at the European Stability Initiative, told Al Jazeera.

“Casting Bosnia as a front-line in a supposed war between Christianity and Islam, and himself as a defender of Christian Europe, is aimed at the one people in Europe against whom a genocide has been committed since the Second World War and recognised as such by two international courts,” he added.

Cerimagic added that Dodik’s rhetoric may reflect uncertainty over the electoral prospects of his preferred candidate, as well as a belief that the European Union has less leverage over Bosnia than it once did.

Initial results are customarily released by the Central Election Commission late on election night and then refreshed every few hours.

In the days that follow, the commission progressively inputs votes from polling stations that remain outstanding, mobile voting teams, as well as ballots sent by mail and those cast at diplomatic and consular missions.

The final, official results must be published by November 20 at the latest.

articles.title: The new Israel-Syria deal: Can US solve the Golan Heights problem?
articles.summary: The Golan Heights dispute returned to the centre of the diplomatic spotlight at the United Nations General Assembly in September 2026, when Syrian
articles.body: The Golan Heights dispute returned to the centre of the diplomatic spotlight at the United Nations General Assembly in September 2026, when Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa declared that the territory “will remain Syrian”, while Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu invoked its biblical links to defend Tel Aviv’s claim.Addressing the UN on September 23, al-Sharaa accused Israel of violating Syrian sovereignty through more than 500 air and artillery strikes, over 1,200 land incursions and nearly 300 detentions since the fall of Bashar al-Assad in December 2024. He called for Israeli forces to withdraw to the lines held on December 8, 2024, and reaffirmed Syria’s commitment to the 1974 disengagement agreement. He also rejected what he described as Israel’s attempt to impose a “fait accompli”, saying that the Golan would remain Syrian territory.A day later, Netanyahu responded directly to al-Sharaa during his own UN General Assembly address. “Mr. al-Sharaa, you should know the Jews have been on the Golan Heights since the days of Moses. You can read it in the Bible,” he said, invoking Israel’s historical and religious links to the plateau.The exchange captured the central challenge facing Washington as it attempts to broker a new security arrangement between the two countries. The US wants to reduce tensions along the Israel-Syria border and create conditions for wider diplomatic engagement. But the disagreement is no longer confined to the Golan Heights, which Israel captured from Syria in 1967 and annexed in 1981. Since Assad’s fall in December 2024, Israeli forces have established positions inside southern Syria, while Damascus has demanded their withdrawal.The violence in the Druze-majority province of Suwayda in July 2025 has added another layer of mistrust, raising questions about whether a border agreement can address Israel’s concerns over the treatment of minorities. Washington may be able to negotiate security zones and monitoring arrangements. Whether it can bridge the two countries’ competing claims over territory, sovereignty and security is a much harder question.Why the Golan remains a central disputeThe Golan Heights is a strategic plateau overlooking northern Israel and southern Syria. Its elevated terrain offers military and surveillance advantages, making it important to Israel’s defence planning. Israel captured the territory from Syria during the 1967 Arab-Israeli war and extended its law and administration to it in 1981.That annexation was rejected by the United Nations and most of the international community. UN Security Council Resolution 497, adopted on December 17, 1981, declared Israel’s decision to impose its laws and administration on the Golan “null and void” and without international legal effect. The UN continues to regard the territory as occupied Syrian land.The United States departed from its previous position on March 21, 2019, when then-President Donald Trump announced that Washington would recognise Israeli sovereignty over the Golan. The decision reversed decades of US policy, but did not change the position of the UN or most countries. Colombia’s recognition of Israel’s claim in August 2026 made it the second country to do so, according to reports.The dispute has endured even during periods when the border remained relatively quiet. Syria has continued to claim the territory, but has not made a serious military attempt to retake it in recent decades. The 1974 disengagement agreement, signed after the 1973 Arab-Israeli war, established a separation zone and restrictions on military deployments, monitored by the United Nations Disengagement Observer Force (UNDOF).That arrangement helped contain direct confrontation, but it did not settle the question of sovereignty. This distinction is central to the current negotiations: a security agreement could regulate military activity without resolving who owns the Golan.What Washington wants from a new agreementThe Trump administration is pushing for a security arrangement that could reduce the risk of conflict along the Israel-Syria border. Washington sees such an agreement as a possible first step towards wider diplomatic engagement, including eventual normalisation and Syria’s entry into the Abraham Accords.The proposed framework, as described in reporting and analysis, would involve a demilitarised zone across southern Syria, a return towards the 1974 disengagement lines, guarantees for the Druze community and an Israeli withdrawal from positions established inside Syrian territory after Assad’s fall. The question of Golan sovereignty would be postponed rather than resolved.The approach reflects a familiar diplomatic calculation: address immediate security concerns first and leave the most politically difficult territorial issue for later. Israel could receive assurances that Syrian forces would not approach the border in strength, while Damascus could maintain that it had not formally surrendered its claim to the Golan.But the two sides disagree over the sequence and terms. Damascus wants Israeli forces to return to the positions they held before December 8, 2024, and says it should retain the right to rebuild its military and determine its alliances. Israel, meanwhile, wants security guarantees and restrictions on military activity in southern Syria before giving up positions it considers valuable.The negotiations have come close to an understanding, but have not produced a durable agreement. Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani said in August 2026 that the two sides had agreed on paper to “almost everything” around the beginning of the year, including arrangements for security zones in southern Syria. But Damascus doubted Israel’s willingness to implement the proposed deal.Why Israel wants military positions inside SyriaIsrael’s military presence inside Syria expanded after Assad was toppled in December 2024. Israeli forces moved into areas near the Golan and the UN-patrolled buffer zone, while Israel also struck Syrian military facilities and other targets. Israel has described these actions as defensive measures intended to prevent threats from emerging near its border.The positions offer more than a physical buffer. They can provide observation over approaches to the Golan, improve Israel’s ability to monitor movement in southern Syria and give its military more time to respond to potential threats. The terrain around Mount Hermon is particularly important because elevated ground offers a broad view of surrounding territory.The military presence also gives Israel leverage in negotiations. A withdrawal can become part of a broader bargain involving security guarantees, limits on Syrian military deployments and monitoring mechanisms. From Israel’s perspective, leaving without enforceable assurances could mean giving up a strategic advantage while relying on a government whose future conduct remains uncertain.For Damascus, however, the same positions represent an infringement on sovereignty. Syria argues that Israel should withdraw from territory it entered after Assad’s fall before the two sides discuss a longer-term security arrangement.The disagreement was underscored on September 9, 2026, when Netanyahu visited an Israeli military position on Mount Hermon, inside Syrian territory. He said Israel had established “absolute control” over an area stretching from the mountain’s summit south to the Yarmouk River and west to the Mediterranean Sea. Syrian officials condemned the visit as a violation of the country’s sovereignty and territorial integrity.The RSIS analysis published on September 17, 2026, said a framework under discussion included an Israeli withdrawal from nine outposts established inside the Syrian Golan over the preceding year. These positions have therefore become a test of whether the two sides can translate diplomatic understandings into a change on the ground.The Suwayda crisis: The obstacle beyond the GolanThe violence in Suwayda in July 2025 exposed a problem that a border agreement may not be able to solve. The province, in southern Syria, has a large Druze population. A local conflict escalated after government forces entered the area, widening into a crisis involving government troops, tribal fighters and Druze armed groups.A United Nations inquiry later put the death toll above 1,700, most of them Druze civilians, and said that government troops, tribal fighters and Druze militias may have committed war crimes. Israel intervened militarily, striking the Defence Ministry in Damascus and government forces near Suwayda. It said its actions were intended to protect the Druze community.The episode matters because it shaped Israel’s assessment of the new Syrian authorities. If Damascus uses force against a minority community, Israel may see a reason to intervene regardless of what happens along the Golan border. In that scenario, a demilitarised zone could reduce the risk of a conventional military clash but would not prevent a crisis elsewhere in Syria from drawing Israel in.A September 17, 2026, analysis by the S. Rajaratnam School of International Studies argued that Washington may be misdiagnosing the central obstacle by focusing too heavily on Golan demilitarisation. Its assessment is that the deeper issue is whether the Syrian government can be trusted not to coerce or attack minority communities. A security agreement could establish rules between two states, but it could not guarantee how Damascus would treat its own citizens.This is also where proposed guarantees for the Druze become difficult. A written commitment may be possible, but enforcing it would require clarity about who monitors violations, what happens if Syrian forces enter the province and whether Israel would retain the right to intervene. Those questions go beyond the technical design of a border arrangement.Al-Sharaa’s position: Security first, Golan later?Al-Sharaa has signalled that Syria is willing to discuss security arrangements, but has resisted any suggestion that Damascus can abandon its claim to the Golan.In April 2026, he indicated that Syria could discuss the Golan at a later stage if Israel withdrew from territory seized after Assad’s fall. His September 23 address at the UN, however, left little doubt that Damascus would not accept a settlement that treated the Golan as territory Washington could allocate.Al-Sharaa invoked Security Council Resolution 497 and called on international partners to abide by it. He also reaffirmed Syria’s commitment to the 1974 agreement and demanded that Israeli forces withdraw to the lines held on December 8, 2024, the day Assad was removed from power.His position reflects a domestic political constraint. Any Syrian leader who appears to surrender the Golan would face opposition, particularly after years of conflict and foreign intervention. Al-Sharaa has therefore tried to separate the immediate security question from the long-term sovereignty dispute.At an Atlantic Council event on September 22, 2026, he said negotiations with Israel had resolved nearly 90% of the outstanding issues needed for a security agreement. He also joked that he had asked Trump why he did not give Israel New Jersey instead of the Golan. The remarks suggested that Damascus was still open to an agreement, but not to giving up its territorial claim.Netanyahu’s position: Security zones and sovereigntyNetanyahu’s UN remarks reinforced Israel’s refusal to relinquish its claim to the Golan. By invoking Jewish presence there since the days of Moses, he placed the dispute within a historical and religious framework, rather than treating it only as a question of military control.Israel’s immediate security position is also tied to its expanded military presence in southern Syria. Defence Minister Israel Katz said in response to al-Sharaa that the Golan under Israeli sovereignty was “an inseparable part of the State of Israel forever”. He also said Israel would remain on Mount Hermon and in the security zone as long as it perceived a jihadist threat near its border.The remarks underline the gap between the two governments. Syria wants Israeli forces to withdraw to pre-December 2024 lines and restore the 1974 arrangement. Israel wants to retain strategic positions and security zones until it is satisfied that threats from Syrian territory have been removed.That difference also complicates Washington’s role. The US can press Israel to redeploy, but it must also address Israeli concerns about the security environment in southern Syria. At the same time, it cannot expect Damascus to accept an open-ended Israeli military presence as the price of negotiations.The Turkey factor complicates Washington’s taskThe Israel-Syria negotiations are also taking place against the backdrop of growing tension between Israel and Turkey. Ankara is a major regional backer of the new Syrian authorities and has an interest in helping rebuild Syria’s military and state institutions. Israel, meanwhile, is wary of Turkish military influence near its borders and has opposed the possibility of Turkish forces operating at Syrian bases.The issue came into focus in August 2026, when Israel struck the Abu al-Duhur airbase in northwestern Syria. Israel said the strike was intended to prevent a Turkish military deployment, while Syria and Turkey denied that such a deployment was planned. The episode showed how a bilateral Israel-Syria agreement could be affected by a third country’s role in Syria.For Washington, this creates a difficult balancing act. It wants to prevent Israeli-Turkish competition from destabilising Syria, while also encouraging Damascus to accept security arrangements that Israel considers necessary. But restrictions on Syria’s military partnerships could be seen in Damascus as an attempt to limit its sovereignty and dictate its regional relationships.The challenge is therefore larger than drawing a new line on a map. Washington must find a formula that addresses Israel’s concerns without turning southern Syria into a zone where Damascus has limited control over its own security policy.Can Washington solve the Golan problem?Washington can help the two sides reach a practical security agreement. It can mediate a return to the 1974 disengagement framework, negotiate monitoring arrangements, define limits on military deployments and establish channels to prevent incidents from escalating. It can also use diplomatic pressure and incentives to encourage Israeli withdrawal from positions established after December 2024.But the United States cannot make the underlying political dispute disappear. Trump’s 2019 recognition of Israeli sovereignty over the Golan has narrowed Washington’s room to act as a neutral mediator on the territorial question. The UN and most of the international community continue to regard the territory as occupied Syrian land, while Israel considers its control essential to national security.Nor can Washington guarantee that future violence inside Syria will not trigger Israeli intervention. The Suwayda crisis demonstrated that Israel’s security calculations extend beyond the immediate border. If Damascus is accused of targeting minorities, a deal focused only on demilitarisation may prove inadequate.The most realistic outcome may therefore be a limited security arrangement rather than a comprehensive peace agreement. Such a deal could reduce the risk of accidental clashes, establish communication channels and clarify military restrictions. It could also create space for future talks on the Golan. But it would not amount to normalisation, and it would not settle the question of sovereignty.The UN exchange between al-Sharaa and Netanyahu showed how far apart the two sides remain. For Syria, the Golan is a matter of sovereignty and international law. For Israel, it is tied to history, security and the military control of strategic terrain. Washington may be able to negotiate a temporary compromise, but a lasting settlement will depend on whether both governments are willing to accept security guarantees without demanding that the other abandon its core position.You use AI every day. articles.title: Riley Green fills the freezer after scoring a massive bull elk with a bow in the Utah mountains
articles.summary: Riley Green's Instagram photos reveal the massive bull elk he took with a compound bow in the Utah mountains, proving the freezer is officially full.
articles.body: Riley Green has officially taken care of the grocery shopping for a while. The country star traded the stage for the Utah mountains recently, and the trip ended with Green standing behind an absolute stud of a bull elk — one he took with a compound bow. CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE FROM OUTKICK OUTDOORS "Freezer is full," Green wrote Friday on Instagram. "Not many things challenge you like bow hunting elk… thankful for a few days to chase em in the Utah mountains and that I was able to put it all together on an awesome bull." And awesome might be underselling it a bit. The photos Green shared show a huge, mature bull with an impressive rack. He also showed what it looks like to lug all that meat out of the mountains, which is a monumental task in itself. If you've followed Green outside of country music, none of this should come as much of a surprise. He's a longtime hunter and particularly serious about doing it with a bow. In fact, Green is a regular guest host for "Major League Bowhunter," and the show previously followed him through a Montana elk hunt appropriately titled "3rd Times A Charm." He's also talked about just how difficult it is to fit an archery elk hunt around life on the road. During a previous appearance on "Bussin' With The Boys," Green explained that the short season and the time required to actually find and get on elk make bowhunting them especially tricky with a touring schedule. He recalled drawing elk tags in consecutive years but having only a few days available to hunt. COUNTRY MUSIC STAR SAM BARBER BAGS A MONSTER CARIBOU ON HIS RECENT ALASKA HUNTING TRIP That's part of what makes his latest Utah bull so impressive. Unlike rifle hunting, bowhunting requires getting much closer to an elk before taking the shot. And we're talking about an animal that can weigh hundreds of pounds, cover a whole lot of mountainous country and has absolutely no interest in making your life easy. Apparently Green managed to put all the pieces together this time. Country music is having a pretty good elk season Funny enough, Green isn't even the only country star to fill a freezer with Utah elk meat lately. Luke Combs recently tagged a bull of his own during a Utah hunt with Jason Phelps — the same hunt Combs credited with helping motivate his recent 30-pound weight loss. Combs had hoped to get his elk with a bow but ultimately switched to a rifle before getting it done. SIGN UP FOR THE DAILY OUTKICK NEWSLETTER Green, meanwhile, stuck with the bow. Not that we're keeping score here. Love all things hunting and outdoors? Follow OutKick OutDoors on Instagram and TikTok!
